title: macOS Keychain
html:
macOS Keychain

Main Keychains

  • The User Keychain (~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db), which is used to store user-specific credentials like application passwords, internet passwords, user-generated certificates, network passwords, and user-generated public/private keys.
  • The System Keychain (/Library/Keychains/System.keychain), which stores system-wide credentials such as WiFi passwords, system root certificates, system private keys, and system application passwords.[1]
  • It's possible to find other components like certificates in /System/Library/Keychains/*
  • The per-user data protection keychain appears as Local Items or iCloud in Keychain Access. It is separate from login.keychain-db and includes both local-only and synchronizable items; security is primarily a file-based-keychain tool, so a short dump-keychain result does not rule out credentials here.[5]
  • In iOS there is only one Keychain located in /private/var/Keychains/. This folder also contains databases for the TrustStore, certificates authorities (caissuercache) and OSCP entries (ocspache).
  • Apps will be restricted in the keychain only to their private area based on their application identifier.

Password Keychain Access

A copied file-based keychain is not plaintext. Offline decryption of its protected items needs the keychain password or equivalent key material; Chainbreaker targets this format.[1] This is different from a live read in an unlocked user session, where item access controls may allow the read or trigger a prompt without requiring the login password again. The data protection keychain has a different protection and access-group model.[5]

Keychain Entries Protections

File-based keychain ACLs

The SecAccess ACL and partition-list rules below describe file-based keychains. Data protection keychain items instead use code-signing access groups and optional SecAccessControl conditions; do not infer their accessibility from a file-based ACL dump.[5]

Each entry in a file-based keychain is governed by Access Control Lists (ACLs) which dictate who can perform various actions on the keychain entry, including:[1][2]

  • kSecACLAuthorizationExportClear: Allows the holder to get the clear text of the secret.
  • kSecACLAuthorizationExportWrapped: Allows the holder to get the clear text encrypted with another provided password.
  • kSecACLAuthorizationAny: Allows the holder to perform any action.

The ACLs are further accompanied by a list of trusted applications that can perform these actions without prompting. This could be:[1]

  • Nil (no authorization required, everyone is trusted)
  • An empty list (nobody is trusted)
  • List of specific applications.

Also the entry might contain the key kSecACLAuthorizationPartitionID, which is used to identify the teamid, apple, and cdhash.[1][2]

  • If the teamid is specified, the application must have the same teamid to access the entry value without a prompt.
  • If the apple is specified, then the app needs to be signed by Apple.
  • If the cdhash is indicated, then app must have the specific cdhash.

Creating a file-based keychain entry

When a new entry is created using Keychain Access.app, the following rules apply:[1]

  • All apps can encrypt.
  • No apps can export/decrypt (without prompting the user).
  • All apps can see the integrity check.
  • No apps can change ACLs.
  • The partitionID is set to apple.

When an application creates an entry in the keychain, the rules are slightly different:[1]

  • All apps can encrypt.
  • Only the creating application (or any other apps explicitly added) can export/decrypt (without prompting the user).
  • All apps can see the integrity check.
  • No apps can change the ACLs.
  • The partitionID is set to teamid:[teamID here].

Accessing the Keychain

security

# List keychains
security list-keychains

# Dump all metadata and decrypted secrets (a lot of pop-ups)
security dump-keychain -a -d

# Find generic <PASSWORD> for the "Slack" account and print the secrets
security find-generic-password -a "Slack" -g

# Change the specified entry's PartitionID value
security set-generic-password-partition-list \
  -s "test service" -a "test account" \
  -S 'apple-tool:,apple:,teamid:TEAMID' \
  -k 'KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD' ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db

# Dump specifically the <USERNAME> keychain
security dump-keychain ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db

-S sets the item's partition list, while -k supplies the current Keychain password required to make that change; the password-taking flag is deprecated.[4] A successful update does not prove that a later read will be silent: one observed, disabled prototype still triggered a confirmation prompt when it queried the item through Security.framework. A matching partition ID is only one part of the ACL and trusted-application checks described above, so verify the actual read path.[3]

APIs

Tip

The keychain enumeration and dumping of secrets that won't generate a prompt can be done with the tool LockSmith

Other API endpoints can be found in SecKeyChain.h source code.

List and get info about each keychain entry using the Security Framework or you could also check the Apple's open source cli tool security. Some API examples:[1]

  • The API SecItemCopyMatching gives info about each entry and there are some attributes you can set when using it:
  • kSecReturnData: If true, it will try to decrypt the data (set to false to avoid potential pop-ups)
  • kSecReturnRef: Get an object reference for a key, certificate, or identity; password items do not have this object representation. Use kSecReturnPersistentRef to identify a password for a later, targeted query.[6]
  • kSecReturnAttributes: Get metadata about entries
  • kSecMatchLimit: How many results to return
  • kSecClass: What kind of keychain entry

Get ACLs of each entry:[1]

  • With the API SecAccessCopyACLList you can get the ACL for the keychain item. It returns a list of ACLs (such as kSecACLAuthorizationExportClear and the others previously mentioned), where each entry has:[1][2]
  • Description
  • Trusted Application List. This could be:
    • An app: /Applications/Slack.app
    • A binary: /usr/libexec/airportd
    • A group: group://AirPort

Export the data:[1]

  • The API SecKeychainItemCopyContent gets the plaintext
  • The API SecItemExport exports the keys and certificates but might have to set passwords to export the content encrypted

And these are the requirements to be able to export a secret without a prompt:[1]

  • If 1+ trusted apps listed:
  • Need the appropriate authorizations (Nil, or be part of the allowed list of apps in the authorization to access the secret info)
  • Need code signature to match PartitionID
  • Need code signature to match that of one trusted app (or be a member of the right KeychainAccessGroup)
  • If all applications trusted:
  • Need the appropriate authorizations
  • Need code signature to match PartitionID
    • If no PartitionID, then this isn't needed

Caution

Therefore, if there is 1 application listed, you need to inject code in that application.

If apple is indicated in the partitionID, you could access it with osascript so anything that is trusting all applications with apple in the partitionID. Python could also be used for this.

Two additional attributes

  • Invisible: It's a boolean flag to hide the entry from the UI Keychain app[1]
  • General: It's to store metadata (so it's NOT ENCRYPTED)[1]
  • Microsoft was storing in plain text all the refresh tokens to access sensitive endpoint.[1]

Data protection keychain: enumerate, then query one item

Run SecItemCopyMatching from a signed app in the target user's login context with kSecUseDataProtectionKeychain: true; do not assume security dump-keychain or a default SecItem query searched this store. The caller sees only its authorized access groups.[5]

If testing code runs inside another process, its data protection keychain access follows that host executable's entitlements. Inspect the actual signed entitlements with codesign -d --entitlements - /path/to/Target.app and see macOS code-signing entitlements for related checks.[7]

First request attributes only for one item class. kSecAttrSynchronizableAny includes both local and iCloud-synchronizable matches; omitting it excludes synchronizable items.[8] kSecUseAuthenticationUISkip avoids authentication UI during broad enumeration, at the cost of skipping protected matches.[9] Repeat with kSecClassInternetPassword if needed.

import Security
let query: [String: Any] = [
    kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
    kSecUseDataProtectionKeychain as String: true,
    kSecAttrSynchronizable as String: kSecAttrSynchronizableAny,
    kSecMatchLimit as String: kSecMatchLimitAll,
    kSecReturnAttributes as String: true,
    kSecUseAuthenticationUI as String: kSecUseAuthenticationUISkip
]
var result: CFTypeRef?
let status = SecItemCopyMatching(query as CFDictionary, &result)
print(status)
if status == errSecSuccess, let items = result as? [[String: Any]] {
    for item in items { print(item) }
}

For a permitted secret read, build a new, narrow query for the selected item (for example, class, service and account), set kSecReturnData: true and kSecMatchLimit: kSecMatchLimitOne, and expect item-specific authentication or an error. Do not combine kSecReturnData with kSecMatchLimitAll for password items.[10] An errSecItemNotFound result can also reflect the wrong store, sync filter, or missing access-group entitlement rather than an absent credential.[5][7][8]
